And there have definitely been times where I was right and he admits later he should have listened to me. But we're a couple of months away from our twenty-year anniversary (twenty-three years together, which is half my life!), so while we had some tumultuous years in our first decade or so--we even considered splitting at one point, about seven/eight years in (the seven-year-itch is real, IMO)--most of that was ironed out and left behind years ago now. We still fight maybe once a year or so, because sometimes it happens, but generally now we don't get to that point.

The way I see it is, if I wanted to, I could get him to do just about anything. If I really make a sticking point of it, or use my feminine wiles or whatever, he'll give in. But if I do that too often, it'll stop working, and if I do it too often, he'll resent it and me--and I would probably lose some respect for him, along the way, which is ridiculous but I'm sure you understand. So I see it as having a limited number of absolute vetos or votes or whatever, and I need to use that limited number very carefully. When issues come up on which we disagree, I think to myself, "Is this really that big a deal? Is it really something I'm willing to go all the way on?"

And more than that, I ask myself if I'm really so sure I'm right, if I'm really so sure he's wrong, and if my being so sure means i really think my judgment on this is better than his. Do I really trust his judgment so little? Do I really think mine is so much better on this subject, do I really have more information about it than he does? Do I really think if we do it his way, disaster will follow?

And I rarely do, and it rarely is. In fact, it almost never is.

So that's kind of how I learned to stop needing to be the one with the final say or the one who gets the last word. When I realized that I could get him to do anything, that was the same moment I realized that I didn't need to. Every decision he makes is made because he truly think it will be the best for all of us. Once I accepted that and really understood it, that made a big difference. Once I saw letting him have his way as a decision I made rather than a decision he took from me, that made a huge difference. (And once I learned to phrase my disagreement as questions, too, that made a difference in how we related to each other when disagreements came up; I learned that often the issue wasn't so much that we disagreed, it was that we didn't fully understand each others's position.)

I also made his happiness and security, and him feeling like he was in control, my top priority. Not above my own happiness, I don't want to sound like a martyr, and I'm certainly not suggesting you or anyone else turn themselves into doormats, but I realized it was more important to him to feel like he was in control than it was to me to feel like I was. So as long as he feels/felt like he was the one who would ultimately make the decision and I would support his decision, it was easier and more pleasant for me to voice my disagreement--and he was a lot more willing to listen, when I did.

And I make sure to thank him semi-regularly for all he does for us, for taking such good care of us, for working so hard for us, for being such a good man. I learned a long time ago--and I teach my daughters this--that the real way to a man's heart is to make him feel like a man, basically, and as long as you do that, everything else generally follows quite pleasantly. What's the line from The Godfather, "Women and children can be irresponsible. Man can't?"
